clue.text: Son, clumsy, far from alert

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a son who is both clumsy and dozy.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it read as a list of a boy's faults; in fact the first two items build the answer and the third defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sleeper is unconscious, the opposite of alert.

clue.text: Git given a fizzy drink

parts.note: git and sod are both British insults for an unpleasant person

explanation.surface: Someone unpleasant is handed a fizzy drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Git and sod are mild British terms of abuse for an annoying man.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is carbonated water, the standard fizzy drink.

clue.text: Regularly unteach Mormons found in this state

indicators.note: at regular intervals: take every other letter

explanation.surface: A hint that missionaries in some state are unlearning their teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue: Utah is the state most associated with the Mormon church, whose headquarters are in Salt Lake City.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah was settled by Mormons and is still the centre of the Latter-day Saint church.

clue.text: Sweet book with Sussex setting …

definitions.meaning: a stick of rock sold at a Sussex seaside resort
Graham Greene's 1938 novel, set on the Sussex coast

explanation.surface: A description of a novel set in southern England.
explanation.walkthrough: Rock is a hard, cylindrical British seaside sweet with the resort's name running through it; Brighton is a resort in Sussex. The ellipsis carries the answer into 4 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Brighton rock is both the seaside sweet and the title of Greene's Brighton-set novel.

clue.text: … agreed, that's an extract from it

indicators.note: an extract is a passage lifted out of a longer text, so the answer is lifted out of the middle of 'it'

parts.note: 'it' is the answer to 3 down; drop its first letter and its last four

explanation.surface: Continuing 3 down: a reader agrees that a passage comes from the novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' points back across the ellipsis to 3 down, so the letters sit inside that answer, b-RIGHT ON-rock, not inside this clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the exclamation 'right on!' voices hearty agreement.

clue.text: Safari centre sees Everyman fatigue abrupt Scotsman after capsizing

indicators.note: cut short: the last letter of bore is lopped off
capsizing turns a boat upside down; in a down clue the assembled letters are turned over, bottom to top

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as I
bore = fatigue, weary; cut short to BOR
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: A travelling Scotsman collapses from exhaustion somewhere on safari.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself in a clue usually means I or ME. Nairobi, Kenya's capital, is the usual starting point for East African safaris.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is where most Kenyan safaris begin.

clue.text: Possesseth headgear, 'tis put on horse

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Olde-worlde talk about putting a hat on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic -eth of the definition asks for an archaic answer, and 'tis keeps the period flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Hath is the old third-person form of has, just as possesseth is of possesses.

clue.text: Accepting only some commands of orthodontists etc

indicators.note: take only some of the letters that follow

parts.note: the letters run from the end of 'commands', through 'of', into the start of 'orthodontists'

explanation.surface: A patient who follows only some of the dentist's orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the abbreviation tacked on the end, which reads as a lazy close to the sentence. The answer spans comm-ANDS OF ORTH-odontists.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: etc stands for et cetera, Latin for 'and the rest'.

clue.text: Fake some deaths where people might be living

indicators.note: faked letters are forged into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone faking deaths, perhaps an insurance fraud, in places where people live.
explanation.walkthrough: The contrast of deaths and living hides that the middle two words are simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A homestead is a house with its land, a place where people live.

clue.text: Pulling wrestling move that binds

definitions.note: 'that binds' stands for a noun, a thing that binds

parts.note: a pin holds an opponent's shoulders to the mat

explanation.surface: A wrestler's hold that ties up the opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one wrestling hold, but it splits after 'Pulling'. A drawing pin is the British name for a thumbtack.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing pin fastens paper to a board, so it is a thing that binds.

clue.text: First man to block America First

parts.note: its first letter, which the clue's closing word also puts first
to dam a river is to block it

explanation.surface: A political slogan and someone trying to stop it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'America First' looks like the slogan, but it gives A and says where A goes; 'First' does double duty with the definition's 'First'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: in Genesis, Adam is the first human God makes.

clue.text: Shrinking baked good: it'll keep you in shape

explanation.surface: A diet tip about a baked treat that won't ruin your figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrinking' and 'keep you in shape' pull towards dieting; shrinking here means shy, and the shape is a tucked gymnastic one.
explanation.definitionFit: A backward roll is a gymnastic exercise, done tucked into a ball.

clue.text: Angry Charlotte and King Edward's unwanted issues

parts.note: Charlotte and King Edward are British potato varieties

explanation.surface: A cross Charlotte and a king with problems nobody wants.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte and King Edward read as royalty, but both are potato varieties sold in British shops; together they are potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot potato is a controversial issue nobody wants to handle.

clue.text: Director, light-hearted fellow, equips places with milkmaids

explanation.surface: A cheerful film director kitting out rustic locations.
explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces in clue order; the only trap is taking 'light-hearted fellow' as one person.
explanation.definitionFit: Milkmaids work where cows are milked, on dairy farms.

clue.text: Inflamed, each lech's mostly shown involuntary movement

indicators.note: most of the word: drop its last letter

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A furious account of a lecherous man's twitching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A pop' is informal for each, as in 'a pound a pop'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apoplectic means furious, inflamed with anger.

clue.text: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally, principally?

definitions.text: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally, principally?

indicators.note: take the principal, that is first, letters

parts.words: A long, powerful harmonic object rendered naturally
parts.note: the first letter of each of the seven words

explanation.surface: A description of a long horn played without valves.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both spells the answer and describes it: an alphorn is a long wooden horn with no valves, so it plays only natural harmonics.
explanation.definitionFit: The alphorn is a very long, loud Alpine horn sounding the natural harmonic series.

clue.text: Tedious far side of Stromboli, disruptive smoker

indicators.note: the letters are disrupted into a new order
the far end of the word, its last letter

explanation.surface: Complaining about a smoking volcano on a dreary stretch of coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Stromboli is a constantly erupting volcanic island off Sicily, so a 'smoker' there reads as the volcano, not the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Irksome means annoying and tiresome.

clue.text: They describe pupils' behaviour: explosions, gunshot, etc

definitions.meaning: documents sent home at the end of a school term

explanation.surface: A teacher's note on unruly pupils, as if the classroom were a battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: School reports are written assessments sent home to parents; a report is also the bang of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Reports are both school assessments and loud bangs.

clue.text: Magnificent muesli in mix bachelor's ingested

indicators.note: the letters are put in a mix, scrambled

parts.note: B = bachelor, as in BA; it goes inside the mixed letters

explanation.surface: Praise for a muesli mix a single man has eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: Breakfast words make 'mix' and 'ingested' look like eating, but they are the two instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sublime means supremely fine, magnificent.

clue.text: Ripped off like a dart

explanation.surface: Robbed as sharply and quickly as a thrown dart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a dart' reads as a simile for speed; it is literal, a dart being built with a shaft.
explanation.definitionFit: Shafted is slang for cheated or ripped off; a dart is shafted in having a shaft.

clue.text: Poet, husky in voice?

indicators.note: 'in voice' means as uttered by the voice, so the word is said, and what you hear is spelt differently

explanation.surface: Asking whether a poet has a rough voice.
explanation.walkthrough: Husky suggests a hoarse voice, but here it means covered in husks or shells, so shelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English Romantic poet.

clue.text: Euros for brioche?

definitions.meaning: bread is slang for money, and euros are the money of France
a rich, buttery loaf from France

explanation.surface: Asking what you might pay for a brioche.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread is old slang for money, so the currency of France is literally French bread; the question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Brioche is a type of loaf from France; euros are money in France, and bread is slang for money.

clue.text: Miserable poet on the up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading bottom to top

parts.note: a bard is a poet, especially a Celtic one

explanation.surface: A gloomy poet whose fortunes are rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the up' sounds like improving prospects, at odds with 'Miserable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Drab means dull and cheerless.

clue.text: Tennis legend showing evidence of fire and energy

parts.note: ash is what a fire leaves

explanation.surface: A tennis great playing with fire and energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975; 'fire and energy' reads as praise of his game.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was a champion American tennis player.

clue.text: As delivered, proper ceremony

indicators.note: as a speech is delivered, spoken

explanation.surface: A formal ceremony performed correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As delivered' could mean as handed over; here it means as spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rite is a formal act performed as part of a ceremony.

clue.text: Hoarding William's canned food

definitions.note: 'Hoarding' is singular in form; the answer is plural

indicators.note: put in a can: one piece holds the other

parts.note: board = meals, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: William stockpiling tinned food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarding' reads as stockpiling, but it is the British word for a large advertising board, a billboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarding is a billboard; the singular stands for the plural answer as a mass noun.

clue.text: Nauseous, oily, not a little lugubrious

indicators.note: 'not' negates, so the letter that follows is taken out of the word

parts.note: slick = oily, as in an oil slick

indicators.note: a little of the word, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of lugubrious, removed from SLICK

explanation.surface: Feeling queasy and greasy, and more than a little gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: Three adjectives look like a list of symptoms; only the first is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nauseous describes the queasy feeling of being about to be ill.

clue.text: 'Cyber-'? 'E-'? Call out what some junk may be!

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: Puzzling over prefixes that tag things as online, then naming what junk might be.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and hyphens make 'Cyber-' and 'E-' look like prefixes to attach; they are just letters. 'Call out' reads as a phrase meaning shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Much household junk can be recycled.
